growth_story.headline: Bananas faded, crisis and disasters stalled growth after 2008, and since 2016 building, rebuilding and tourism have lifted income per person to a new high.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2007 income per person grew 3.7 percent a year, even as the European trade preferences behind banana exports, once a large share of goods exports, lost value from the early 1990s. Growth then stalled at 0.7 percent a year from 2008 to 2015, as the global financial crisis weakened the economy and a run of natural disasters, including the floods of December 2013, kept cutting short the recovery. Since 2016 growth has averaged 3.0 percent a year, well above the 1.7 of the decade before. That era held hard shocks: the pandemic cut income per person by 3.7 percent in 2020, La Soufrière erupted in 2021, and Hurricane Beryl struck in 2024. It still ended with three strong years, 6.1, 4.8 and 4.1 percent from 2023 to 2025, carried by large public and hotel projects, rebuilding and a tourism rebound, and in 2025 income per person reached its highest level on record. The sources describe the same years as ones of wide deficits and fast-rising public debt, with building now slowing as the big projects finish.

threads.title: Banana preferences fade
threads.text: Bananas sold to Europe under trade preferences were long a large share of goods exports. The value of those preferences peaked in the early 1990s and then fell steeply, and IMF research finds the loss hit growth hardest in the islands that relied on them most, St. Vincent and the Grenadines among them. What kept growth going through 1990 to 2007 is not explained in the sources.

threads.title: Crisis, floods and an airport
threads.text: After 2008 the global financial crisis weakened the economy, and floods, landslides and drought kept cutting short the recovery; income per person fell in 2009, 2010 and 2011. In the same years the government built a new international airport, and its imports, with disaster rebuilding, widened the deficits.

threads.title: Pandemic, then a volcano
threads.text: The pandemic cut tourism sharply in 2020, and income per person fell 3.7 percent. In April 2021 La Soufrière erupted, forcing mass evacuations on the main island and hitting farms hard, yet income per person still rose 2.8 percent that year.

threads.title: Rebuilding, hotels and tourists
threads.text: Large public and private projects and a strong return of tourists drove the recovery after the pandemic and the eruption. Hurricane Beryl in 2024 wrecked most buildings in the southern Grenadines, and rebuilding added to the building boom. The World Bank expects building to slow as new hotels and public works are finished.

since_last_year.text: Over the past year growth has eased from its rebuilding peak. The World Bank (October 2026) says growth slowed in 2025 as rebuilding after Beryl and the big projects passed their peak, while tourist arrivals kept rising. The IMF (June 2026) reports a wide deficit and much higher public debt, and expects slower growth as oil prices rise.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person rising 2.8 percent in 2021, the year of the eruption, while the IMF at the time expected the economy to shrink deeply that year. The data also show income per person at a record high in 2025 after three strong years, while the sources describe those years as a borrowing-funded building boom that is now winding down. The 1990 to 2007 era is the fastest of the three in the data even though the sources describe it as the time banana preferences were lost.
